## The idea

A drum groove is easier to inspect when each instrument has one row on a shared
time grid. Sixteen steps give four subdivisions per beat in 4/4. A hit is true,
a rest is false, and the column number is the event's time.

Start with kick, snare, and closed hi-hat. More samples increase the number of
decisions before the pulse is stable. Separate arrays also support the
transcription method that works best for dense grooves: loop the source and
listen for one instrument at a time.

The grid captures attacks. Amplitude captures accents, and a small sleep offset
can place an instrument ahead of or behind the exact subdivision. Those
performance details should remain visible beside the pattern rather than being
buried in a recorded loop.

## Run this

The hi-hat marks all sixteen steps. Kick and snare occupy selected columns.
Accent arrays make the beat hierarchy audible, and the hat plays 0.02 beats
late.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 100

kick =  [true, false, false, false, false, false, true, false,
         true, false, false, false, false, false, false, false]
snare = [false, false, false, false, true, false, false, false,
         false, false, false, false, true, false, false, false]
hats =  [true, true, true, true, true, true, true, true,
         true, true, true, true, true, true, true, true]
hat_amp = [0.8, 0.35, 0.5, 0.35] * 4

16.times do |step|
  sample :bd_haus, amp: 1.0 if kick[step]
  sample :sn_dub, amp: 0.8 if snare[step]

  in_thread do
    sleep 0.02
    sample :drum_cymbal_closed, amp: hat_amp[step], release: 0.08 if hats[step]
  end

  sleep 0.25
end
```

The kick establishes beats 1 and 3 with an extra pickup before beat 3. The
snare marks beats 2 and 4. The hat accents every beat and sits slightly behind
the kick-snare grid.

## Change one thing

1. Set every hat amplitude to 0.5. The subdivision remains, but the bar loses
   its four-beat shape. Restore the accent pattern before changing any hits.
2. Move the second kick from index 6 to index 7. It now lands one sixteenth
   before beat 3. Listen for a tighter pull into the downbeat.
3. Change the hat offset from 0.02 to 0.06. The delayed layer becomes easier to
   hear and may feel detached. Reduce it until the timing changes the pocket
   without sounding like an error.

## Why it works

Each array is a Boolean function over step number. The renderer asks every
instrument the same question at the same time: is there a hit in this column?
That shared index keeps the layers aligned while allowing independent patterns.
It also makes a paper transcription possible. Draw sixteen columns, mark the
hits, then transfer rows into arrays.

Amplitude is part of the pattern. Equal hi-hats can sound mechanical even when
their positions match a performance. Stronger quarter-note accents reveal the
meter, while weaker offbeats provide motion. Record the values explicitly so a
later editor can see the intended hierarchy.

Microtiming belongs after the grid is correct. A late hat changes the relation
between layers without moving the kick and snare anchors. If every instrument
receives a different offset before the basic transcription is stable, timing
errors become hard to distinguish from style.

Repeated listening works best by isolation. First mark the snare, then kick,
then hats. Mute the rows you are not checking in Sonic Pi. When all rows are
entered, listen for collisions and missing composite accents.

## Take it further

Transcribe one bar of a groove you can legally inspect or record yourself.
Create one sixteen-step array per instrument, plus a parallel amplitude array
where accents differ. Work in separate listening passes and write a REVIEW
comment above uncertain columns. The target is a readable grid that reproduces
the attack pattern without an opaque audio loop. Add timing offsets only after
the strict grid plays correctly, and preserve both versions for comparison.
